volumes.title: The Coal Tin
volumes.text:
I am Odile Farrow, forty years schoolmistress of Emberwick and now nothing in particular. This winter I mean to sit at twelve hearths and collect a tale from each. My terms: one log from my basket for one tale. I also carry a lidded coal tin, to take a live ember on from each fire and lay it in the next, for luck.

I began at the bakery, the oldest fire in town. Tobias Rudd told of Hesper the candlemaker, who settled here before there was a here. Snow fell for a week and she kept one wick burning in her window throughout. Lost carters steered by it, and stayed. Ember Wick, they called the place, and never got round to a better name.

Tobias dropped a coal in my tin. My own parlour grate has been cold since I retired. A fire wants somebody to talk to.

volumes.title: The Cat’s Stone
volumes.text:
Second hearth: Widow Tansley’s on Candle Row, where I carried the baker’s ember in my coal tin and a log of ash in my basket. She has the smallest grate in Emberwick and the largest cat.

Her tale explains the cat. Long ago, she says, a grey cat called Smoke minded a poor family’s fire while they slept. When a coal rolled out, Smoke patted it back with one paw, quick as a wink, and never singed a whisker. The family woke each morning to a house still standing. In thanks they gave her the warmest stone of the hearth, for ever, and her kittens after her.

That is why no Emberwick cat may be moved from the hearthstone, not for a guest, not for the vicar. I sat on the stool. The cat watched me write it all down, and seemed to find it accurate.

volumes.title: The River’s Loan
volumes.text:
The third hearth is hardly a hearth at all: an iron stove in the ferryman’s hut, down where the Ember runs wide and brown. Corwin Dabb took my log, fed my travelling ember a twist of bark to keep it cheerful, and told me this.

His great-grandfather kept the same ferry. One flood night the river rose to the doorstep and carried off his lantern, lit, bobbing away like a duck. He shouted after it that he expected it back. People laughed at that for seven years.

On the seventh spring the lantern was found on the step, upright, still burning, with a little river-weed round the handle. The Ember borrows, Corwin says, but it is an honest river. He showed me the lantern. It is certainly old, and there is weed carved, or grown, about the handle. I did not ask which.

volumes.title: The Hob Who Miscounted
volumes.text:
Fourth hearth, with snow on the lane: the kitchen at Stonecross Mill, where Annis Poole grinds for half the Lowlands. I arrived floury to the knees with my coal tin warm under my shawl.

Every mill has a hob, Annis told me, and theirs lives in the flour bin and counts the sacks. He counts beautifully up to nineteen. The twentieth sack he always misses, however carefully the miller checks him, and so one sack in every score has no owner. It goes to whoever in the parish needs it most, and the hob is never corrected, for fear of hurting his feelings.

I asked if she had seen him. She said no, but she has seen the books, and they have been one sack out in every twenty for two hundred years. As a teacher of arithmetic I ought to disapprove. I find I do not.

volumes.title: The Thirteenth Sheep
volumes.text:
For the fifth hearth I went up into the Northern Fells on the carrier’s cart, coal tin in my lap, to the bothy where Garrick Thwaite winters his flock. His fire is peat, and smells of old rain.

Garrick keeps twelve ewes in the home fold. At dusk, he says, any shepherd on these fells who counts carefully will count thirteen. The extra one is made of mist. She stands a little apart and has no shadow. Leave her be, and on the night a lamb strays she will be gone from the fold, and by morning back again, with the lamb trotting behind her.

We went out at dusk and I counted. Twelve. Garrick said I had counted like a schoolmistress, which is to say too briskly. I tried again, slowly, and shall record only that I stopped at thirteen because I ran out of sheep.

volumes.title: The Kettle That Sang
volumes.text:
Midwinter night, and the sixth hearth is the great one at the Brass Kettle, wide enough to seat four. Half of Emberwick was in. I laid my carried ember in the fire, paid my log, and got my tale from the landlady, Oriel Finch, between pourings.

The inn is named for a kettle that hung here in her grandmother’s day. It sang as it boiled, as kettles do, but this one sang the weather. A high thin note meant frost. A rumbling one meant rain off the Grey Coast. Before snow it hummed like a contented cat, and farmers walked in from three parishes to listen.

A tinker mended its lid one autumn and it never sang true again. It only whistled, like anybody’s. Leave well alone, says Oriel. The kettle still hangs by the chimney, and I took my fresh ember from beneath it.

volumes.title: Boots the Marsh Kept
volumes.text:
The seventh hearth lies out on the marsh, along a causeway of planks, in the reed-cutter’s cottage. Bryony Sedge burns dried reed-roots, which crackle like gossip. I laid in my carried ember, as I do at each house, and asked for a tale.

Everybody who walks the marsh loses one boot to it sooner or later, she said. The mud takes it with a sound like a kiss. Nobody in her family has ever grudged this, because of what happens at midsummer. On the shortest night, every boot lost that year is found standing on the causeway in a row, cleaned, and stuffed with dry moss to keep its shape.

Nobody sees who does it. The frogs are suspected. Bryony’s mother once left out a saucer of milk in thanks and found it returned, washed. I lost no boot myself, though the marsh tried twice going home.

volumes.title: A Knot for Enough
volumes.text:
Eighth hearth: a driftwood fire at the Marlows’ cottage on the Grey Coast, burning blue and green from the salt. I had come nine miles with my coal tin, and old Peg Marlow said the ember in it looked seasick.

She mends nets, and her tale was of a knot. Her grandmother knew a way of tying the last mesh so that a net would hold exactly what a household needed and not a herring more. The extra fish slid through it like water. A neighbour scoffed and tied his own nets tight. He filled his boat so full it would not come over the bar, and had to throw half back.

Peg showed me the knot three times. I can tie a bow and a reef, and I could not follow it. She said that was quite usual, and that it does not work on shopping baskets.

volumes.title: The Giant’s Nightlight
volumes.text:
The ninth hearth is one I know too well: the black stove in the Emberwick schoolroom, which I fed for forty years. Mr Ashby teaches there now. He let me in on a wet afternoon, and the children demanded to know my terms. A log for a tale, I said. They went into a huddle.

Their tale was made up on the spot, with arguments. A giant lived on the Northern Fells who was afraid of the dark. Every evening he reached up and turned the moon so its bright side faced his bed. Some nights he fell asleep before finishing, which is why the moon is so often left half turned.

I asked if a tale invented on a Tuesday counts as folklore. A girl called Nettie said every tale was Tuesday once. I have written that inside the cover of my notebook, and paid the log.

volumes.title: The Honest Nail
volumes.text:
The tenth hearth roars. It is the forge on Anvil Yard, and Hale Orrin would not stop work for me, so I got my tale in pieces between hammer blows, holding my coal tin well back from the sparks.

When the Ember bridge was built, he said, the smith of that day made ten thousand nails for it. One came out crooked. He was going to throw it back in the fire, but the nail spoke up and promised that if it were only given a place it would hold harder than any straight one. So he drove it in under the middle arch.

In the great flood every straight nail groaned. The crooked one held, and the bridge with it. Hale says nobody knows which nail it is, and that this is the point. He gave me an ember with tongs, like a man serving sugar.

volumes.title: The Unfinished Book
volumes.text:
The eleventh hearth is the reading-room fire at Emberwick Library, where the thaw was dripping past the windows. Mrs Larch, the librarian, took my log, shut the door on a draught, and told the last of my borrowed tales.

There was once a book on these shelves, she said, whose final page was blank. Readers complained. The book was sent back to its binder twice. At last an old shelver noticed that the page filled itself, a line at a time, whenever a reader sat by the fire afterwards and told somebody else what they had read. It only wanted the story passed on before it would end.

Then Mrs Larch looked at my coal tin. Eleven hearths lit from one another, she said, and the collector’s own grate stone cold. She said it kindly. Librarians notice an unreturned item.

volumes.title: My Own Hearth
volumes.text:
The twelfth hearth is mine, in the parlour on Chapel Lane, cold since the day I retired. This evening, with the first snowdrops out by the step, I swept the grate, laid kindling, and tipped in the ember from my coal tin. It had passed through eleven fires, from the baker’s oven to the library, and it caught at once.

I had told nobody. All the same there came a knock, and then another. Tobias Rudd with a loaf. Widow Tansley, without the cat. The ferryman, the miller, Bryony Sedge in marsh-stained boots, the smith, Mrs Larch, and half the schoolroom. Each one held out a log. Those were the terms, they said. A log for a tale.

So I told one. It was about a woman who carried a fire round a town all winter before she thought to bring it home. They said it would do.

volumes.title: A Yard of Ribbon
volumes.text:
My name is Ambrose Tull, pedlar of ribbons, buttons and thread, and my round takes me once a month up the Ember valley to the village of Twelvetrees. An old woman there, Granny Sorrel Wick, has never bought so much as a pin from me. Instead she struck a bargain: one yard of green ribbon each visit, in exchange for one part of a tale. Twelve parts, she said. I write them down as I get them.

The first part is short. Before it was Twelvetrees the village was called Nethercombe, and it stood under a bare hill. The old wood had been felled for ship timber in her great-grandmother’s time. After that the wind came through every door without knocking, smoke blew back down the chimneys, and the washing was frequently found in the next parish.

She took her ribbon and said to come back next month.

volumes.title: Twelve Seeds
volumes.text:
At Twelvetrees, for a second yard of green ribbon, Granny Sorrel Wick gave me the second part of her tale of the Green Children. She shelled peas throughout.

In windy Nethercombe, under its bare hill, lived Marra Linden, a charcoal-burner’s widow, which is a hard thing to be where there are no trees. One winter she mended her husband’s old coat and found twelve seeds in the lining. An acorn. An ash key. A hazelnut, a rowan berry dried hard, a holly stone, and seven more she could not name.

She had no use for them and no heart to throw them out. So at the turn of the year she carried them up the hill in her apron, planted them in a ring, and watered each one from the well with her only cup. Then she went home and forgot about them, more or less.

volumes.title: May-Eve Knocking
volumes.text:
I am a pedlar, and Granny Sorrel Wick of Twelvetrees pays me for green ribbon in instalments of story. Third visit, third part.

On May-eve, she said, somebody knocked at Marra Linden’s door, low down, the way a child knocks. Marra was the widow who had planted twelve seeds on the bare hill. On her step stood twelve children, barefoot, very polite, with hair the pale green of new leaves. They asked for nothing but a drink of water.

She had one cup. They passed it round, each taking a sip and saying thank you, and it did not run dry. At dusk they bowed and walked back up the hill in a line. Marra followed in the morning. Where she had planted her ring of seeds there stood twelve saplings, a hand high, and the grass between was trodden flat by small feet.

volumes.title: Children by Day
volumes.text:
Fourth part of the tale of the Green Children, as told to me, Ambrose Tull, by Granny Sorrel Wick, for the usual yard of ribbon.

The rule was soon plain, she said. From sunrise the twelve were children, running about the widow Marra’s cottage. At dusk they climbed the hill and stood as saplings until morning. Rain did not trouble them. They rather leaned into it.

They had no names, so Marra went by their ways. Oak was slow to answer and never wrong. Hazel was quick and wanted to know everything. Willow could not be kept out of the stream. Rowan wore a string of red beads nobody had given her, Birch tidied whatever stood still, and little Holly had sharp elbows and a kind heart. The other six she named as she learned them. It took the whole summer, Granny says, and no summer was better spent.

volumes.title: The Village Makes Up Its Mind
volumes.text:
Fifth visit to Twelvetrees, fifth yard of green ribbon, fifth part. Granny Sorrel Wick told it while darning.

The village of Nethercombe did not take at once to twelve green-haired children who lived with the widow Marra Linden by day and turned into saplings at night. The miller’s wife said they could not be natural, since they ate nothing but rain. The parson said he would think about it, and did, for months.

The children settled the matter themselves. Birch swept the street before breakfast. Willow walked up the dry gully, stamped twice, and found the spring the village had lost sixty years before. Hazel sat at the back of the school and did everyone’s sums. By harvest the miller’s wife was knitting twelve pairs of socks. They were never worn, the children disliking anything between their feet and the ground, but they are in the church chest still.

volumes.title: Holly’s Winter
volumes.text:
It was snowing when I reached Twelvetrees with my pack, and Granny Sorrel Wick made me sit by the fire for the sixth part.

When the leaves fell that first autumn, she said, eleven of the Green Children yawned, climbed the hill, and did not come down again. The widow Marra Linden went up every day and found only bare saplings asleep in the cold. She had got used to a full house.

But one came. Holly, in a dark green coat that shone as if polished, knocked each morning all winter long. She carried the firewood, and when the wind came prowling she stood on the step with her sharp elbows out until it went round. It was a smaller wind already. Twelve saplings are not much of a wood, Granny says, but the wind had noticed them, and was beginning to mind its manners.

volumes.title: A Year in a Season
volumes.text:
Seventh part, seventh yard of ribbon. I am Ambrose Tull, pedlar, and I had the tale of the Green Children from Granny Sorrel Wick of Twelvetrees, who that day was planting beans and talked into the row.

The children grew, she said, as trees do when nobody is watching. They went up the hill one spring evening no higher than Marra Linden’s elbow. By midsummer Oak had to duck under her lintel. The saplings on the hill were head-high and had begun to touch fingers.

Other things came with them. A wren nested in Hazel. Bluebells appeared, though nobody had planted any. The washing stayed on the line. Smoke went up the chimneys of Nethercombe instead of down, and people took to walking on the hill of an evening, for no reason they could give. Marra said the reason was shade. Nobody under forty had ever stood in any.

volumes.title: Mr Crake’s Tape
volumes.text:
Granny Sorrel Wick keeps count on her fingers: this was the eighth part she gave me, for the eighth yard of green ribbon, at Twelvetrees.

One autumn, when the Green Children’s wood stood taller than a haystack, a stranger rode into Nethercombe. He was a Mr Crake, timber-factor to the estate, a neat man with a measuring tape and a small black book. He went round each of the twelve trees, wrote down its girth, and raised his hat to the widow Marra Linden.

The hill, he explained, was timber-ground by an old deed. Whatever grew on it would be felled when it reached a useful size. He was sorry. He would return next harvest-end with men and axes. He was not a cruel man, Granny says. He only believed his book. The children stood very still while he measured them, as children will for a tailor.

volumes.title: Twelve Godparents
volumes.text:
I come to Twelvetrees once a month, and Granny Sorrel Wick trades me her tale for ribbon. This ninth part she told quickly, as though she liked it best.

The estate meant to fell the Green Children’s wood. It was Hazel, the quick one, who found the answer, in a law book she borrowed from the parson. By Lowland custom no axe may touch a tree that has a name and a living godparent.

So the village of Nethercombe held a christening. Twelve households climbed the hill. The miller’s wife stood godmother to Birch. The parson took Oak, having finally made up his mind. Each tree was sprinkled from the widow Marra’s one cup, named aloud, and tied round with a green ribbon so that nobody could say afterwards they had not known. That, Granny said, looking at my pack, is why it has to be green.

volumes.title: Tea with the Factor
volumes.text:
Tenth yard of ribbon, tenth part. I, Ambrose Tull, wrote it down at Granny Sorrel Wick’s table in Twelvetrees.

At harvest-end Mr Crake the timber-factor came back to Nethercombe with his black book. He left the men and axes at the foot of the hill. Twelve trees wore green ribbons. Twelve households stood beside them and recited the custom of godparents, more or less together.

He was asked in to tea at the widow Marra’s. The Green Children sat round the walls. Nobody spoke until Oak, who was slow, asked Mr Crake what tree he had climbed as a boy. A pear tree, he said, in his aunt’s yard. He was quiet for some time. Then he opened his book and wrote across the page: unsuitable for timber. Before he left he asked, rather shyly, if there were any seeds to spare. They gave him a pear pip.

volumes.title: Fewer Knocks
volumes.text:
Granny Sorrel Wick told me the eleventh part slowly, in her doorway at Twelvetrees, winding my eleventh yard of ribbon round her hand.

As the wood grew tall, she said, the Green Children came down the hill less often. Trees have a great deal to attend to. First they missed the wet days, then the weekdays. In the end they came only on May-eve, twelve tall people with grey-green hair, to knock low on Marra Linden’s door from habit and pass her one cup round.

Marra grew old among them and was content. The last May-eve she was too stiff to rise, so they let themselves in. After that they came no more as people. But the wood crept down the hill, year by year, until it stood about her cottage on every side. No wind has got into the village since. That was when Nethercombe changed its name.

volumes.title: The Rowan by the Well
volumes.text:
The twelfth yard of green ribbon bought me the end of the tale, and Granny Sorrel Wick of Twelvetrees walked me through the village to tell it.

Ever since Marra Linden’s day, she said, each child born here has a tree planted and a godparent to stand by it, and all of them are called green children, whatever colour their hair. She stopped at the well and patted a rowan, old and leaning, with eleven of my ribbons on it. She tied on the twelfth. Hers, planted eighty-one years ago.

Then she gave me an acorn. From Oak himself, she said. A pedlar has no ground of his own, so I planted it by the gate of Emberwick Library, where the librarian lets me water it. It is knee-high this spring. It has not knocked at any door yet. I keep a cup handy all the same.

volumes.title: The Stranger’s Rope
volumes.text:
I am Hester Quillfeather, newly appointed keeper of the parish records at Emberwick, and I was raised in a street with paving. The vicar has asked me to write down the harvest customs of the Lowland farms before they are forgotten. I began this morning at Longacre, where they were to cut the first barley.

I had barely stepped through the gate when two reapers came up, smiling, and bound my wrists with a rope of twisted straw. This, I learn, is the Stranger’s Rope. Whoever first enters a harvest field without a tool in hand must pay a forfeit.

Mistress Bell Hathersage, who farms Longacre, set mine herself: one day’s honest work in the field, to be paid before the Lodger sits down to supper. I do not yet know who the Lodger is. I have written it down, and they let me keep the rope.

volumes.title: Whetting the Blades
volumes.text:
Second day at Longacre farm, where I am recording the harvest customs for the parish. Nobody may cut a stalk, I find, until the blades have been whetted in the proper manner.

The oldest reaper and the youngest stand face to face at the field gate. This year they are Jem Purvis, who is seventy-eight, and a boy named Colin, who is eleven and was trying not to grin. Each sharpens the other’s scythe. The old hand gives the young blade its edge and the young hand returns the favour, so that skill goes down the years and strength comes back up them. That is how Jem put it.

Then the first swathe is cut in complete silence, the whole line moving together, so as not to wake the field. I asked what happens if the field wakes. Nobody knew. Nobody has ever been willing to find out.

volumes.title: The Lark’s Acre
volumes.text:
I am Hester Quillfeather, and I follow the reapers at Longacre with a notebook. On the third day the line of scythes stopped dead in the middle of the barley.

A lark had gone up. Jem Purvis walked forward, parted the stalks, and found the nest. He pushed a hazel stick into the ground beside it and tied on a red rag. The reapers then cut round that spot in a wide ring, leaving an island of standing corn about the size of a kitchen table. This is called the Lark’s Acre, though it is nothing like an acre.

There were four such islands by evening. The grain in them is never harvested. It belongs to the lark, in payment for singing over the field all summer. Mistress Hathersage says the lark has never once sent a bill, which is more than can be said for the wheelwright.

volumes.title: The Long Loaf
volumes.text:
Noon in the harvest field at Longacre, where I am recording the Lowland customs. Dinner is carried out by the children in a covered basket, and the chief of it is the Long Loaf.

It is baked the length of a scythe blade, with a curve to it, and takes two to carry. No knife may touch it. A blade that has cut bread in the field, they say, grows soft and will want only bread afterwards. So the loaf is broken, passed hand to hand down the line, eldest first, each tearing a piece. With it go cheese, onions, and cold tea from a stone jug that has stood all morning in the river Ember.

I was handed the loaf in my turn like anyone else. I pointed out that my forfeit of a day’s work was still unpaid. They said the loaf does not keep accounts.

volumes.title: Eight Verses and a Hum
volumes.text:
Behind the reapers at Longacre come the binders, tying the cut barley into sheaves, and the binders sing. I have been set to record the harvest customs, so I sat on the bank and attended closely.

There is one binding song and it has eight verses, because eight sheaves make a stook. A verse lasts as long as it takes a quick pair of hands to gather, twist and tie. The tune is plain and goes up at the end of each line, like a question from a child. By the eighth verse the binder has a stook’s worth at her feet and begins again.

Then there is a ninth verse, which has no words. It is hummed, and it is for the weather. I asked why it has no words. Nan Purvis said the weather does not like to be told things outright. One hums, and hopes.

volumes.title: Three Knots for Weather
volumes.text:
A confession belongs in today’s notes. I am Hester Quillfeather, I record harvest customs, and I have meddled with one.

At Longacre, when the corn is cut but not yet carried, they hang weather knots on the field gate. Each is a wisp of straw tied in a loop, and each asks for one dry day. The rule is strict: never more than three. To ask for four is greedy, and greed fetches thunder.

On Tuesday evening there were three knots on the gate. The sky looked doubtful to me. I thought a fourth could do no harm, and I tied one, rather neatly. It rained for two days. The whole farm sat in the barn mending sacks and wondering aloud who could have done such a thing. Nobody looked at me. They did not look at me so carefully that I am certain they all know.

volumes.title: The Water-Carrier’s Due
volumes.text:
The children of Longacre are not idle at harvest. I have been recording the customs of the farm for the parish, and the smallest custom belongs to the smallest worker.

One child is chosen as water-carrier. This year it is Colin, aged eleven, who walks the field all day with a yoke and two cans, so that no reaper need leave the line. It is hot, dull and heavy work. For it he is owed two things by ancient right, and no farmer has ever dared refuse them.

The first is the earliest ripe apple in the orchard, whoever spots it. The second is the naming of the scarecrow. At the end of harvest the scarecrow is brought in from the field, and the water-carrier announces its name for the coming year. Last year’s was Lord Turnip. Colin says he has decided, and will not be bribed into telling.

volumes.title: The Lodger
volumes.text:
I now know who the Lodger is. I have wondered since my first day at Longacre, when I was bound with a straw rope and told my forfeit must be paid before the Lodger sits down to supper.

The Lodger is the last sheaf. When only one armful of barley stands in the last field, the reapers do not scythe it. Mistress Hathersage cuts it herself, with a small sickle, and binds it thicker than the rest. It is then dressed: an old hat, a waistcoat, a neckerchief. This year’s has a pipe.

The Lodger is carried home in state and lives in the farmhouse kitchen until spring, in the chair nearest the fire. Nobody may be short with it. Its grain is the first sown next year, so that the field, they say, remembers itself. It looks a comfortable sort of person. I still owe my day’s work.

volumes.title: A Day’s Honest Work
volumes.text:
Today I, Hester Quillfeather, keeper of parish records, paid my forfeit. I had owed Longacre farm one day’s honest work since the reapers caught me in their field with the Stranger’s Rope.

It was the last carrying day. I was given a pitchfork and shown how to lift a sheaf onto the wagon. I lifted perhaps two hundred. Roughly forty arrived where I aimed them. One landed on Jem Purvis, who is seventy-eight and said he had been hit by worse. My stooks, built in the morning, were found to be standing on their heads.

No one laughed until I did. At noon I was given first tear of the Long Loaf, which I am told is not custom at all, but manners. I have eleven blisters and have counted them twice. Mistress Hathersage inspected my hands, nodded, and said the debt was paid in full.

volumes.title: The Lantern Load
volumes.text:
The last wagon of the harvest left the field at Longacre this evening, and I walked behind it with my notebook. They call it the Lantern Load, because it must not start for home until dusk.

A lantern is hung on the shafts. The horse wears ribbons, and the children ride on top with the Lodger, the dressed last sheaf, propped among them. The custom concerns the gates. Each gate on the way must be opened by someone who has opened no other gate that day, or the luck stays shut in the field.

There are five gates. Four were soon spoken for. At the farmyard gate everyone looked round and found they had all opened something since breakfast. I had not. I had climbed every stile all day on purpose, having read my own notes. I opened it. The cheer was quite unsuitable for a records office.

volumes.title: The Gleaners’ Bell
volumes.text:
With the fields at Longacre cleared, one harvest custom remains out of doors, and I went to record it. At eight this morning the church bell at Emberwick rang twelve slow strokes. That is the Gleaners’ Bell, and until it sounds no one may set foot on the stubble.

Then the gate is opened, and in they go to gather the fallen ears: widows first, then children, then anyone at all. What they glean is theirs. A quick family may carry home flour for the winter.

I noticed something not in any record. The evening before, Mistress Hathersage’s men had gone over the field with rakes, and they had raked remarkably badly. Whole handfuls lay about. Jem Purvis says a tidy field is a mean field, and the trick is to be careless in the right places. I gleaned a small bag myself. Nobody tied my wrists this time.

volumes.title: The Lodger Sits Down
volumes.text:
Harvest supper was held in the great barn at Longacre last night, and it closes my record of the customs. I came to this farm a stranger in town shoes, and was bound with a straw rope on the first day for it.

The tables ran the length of the threshing floor. Colin the water-carrier announced the scarecrow’s name, which is Sir Hesitant Crow. Then Mistress Hathersage called for the newest hand to carry in the Lodger. Everyone turned to look at me.

So I carried the last sheaf, hat, waistcoat, pipe and all, to its chair by the fire, and it sat down to supper. The straw rope has been plaited into its belt. I meant to write these customs down before they were forgotten. I had not expected to end up inside one. Next year I am to bring my own pitchfork.

volumes.title: The Lamplighter’s Book
volumes.text:
I am Jory Flint, lamplighter of Emberwick. I have forty-one lamps, a ladder, a pole, and a left knee that tells the weather. Every evening I walk the town at dusk, and I have learned that dusk is the hour when people see things. They will not tell the vicar. They will tell the man with the ladder, because he is out in it too.

So I have bought this book to write the sightings down, without deciding whether they are true.

I begin with my own. It is March. My last lamp is number forty-one, at the bottom of Marsh Lane, a long cold walk on a bad knee. Three evenings this week I have come round the bend and found it already burning, the glass shut and the wick trimmed. Nobody was about. I said thank you to the lane in general, and went home.

volumes.title: The Hare That Bows
volumes.text:
Reported to me, Jory Flint, lamplighter, at lamp number six by the church, by the sexton, Mr Enoch Bramble, who is not a fanciful man and wished that put on record.

Most evenings in April a grey hare comes over the fields and sits upon the churchyard wall, facing west. It keeps quite still as the light goes. When the first star shows, it bows. The sexton was firm that it is a bow, with the ears laid back and the head brought down, and not a hare scratching itself. Then it goes home across the glebe.

I lit number six slowly for a week to watch. I saw the hare five evenings out of seven. I saw the bow twice, and once I believe it included me. Being on a ladder at the time, I could only nod. I have entered the hare in my book as punctual.

volumes.title: Good Evening from the Line
volumes.text:
Dusk comes later in May, and I light lamp fourteen on Thimble Lane at half past eight. That is where Mrs Pettibone stopped me to report a thing for my book of sightings.

She leaves her washing out late. On still evenings, she says, when not a leaf is moving, one item on the line will lift and wave. It is always the same one, a blue apron that was her mother’s. It waves three times, as her mother used to from that very door, and hangs quiet again.

I am Jory Flint, the lamplighter, and I know every draught in Emberwick. There is none in that yard. I stood and watched with her. The air was like a held breath, and the apron lifted, once, twice, three times. Mrs Pettibone said good evening to it in an ordinary voice. So I did too. It seemed only civil.

volumes.title: Two Shadows on the Bridge
volumes.text:
The baker’s boy came running to my ladder with something for the book. I am Jory Flint, lamplighter, and I write down what Emberwick sees at dusk. He had crossed the Ember bridge at lighting-up and met the Dusk Folk: long thin people, he said, one walking ahead of him and one behind, who stopped when he stopped.

I took him back and showed him. There is a lamp at each end of the bridge, numbers twenty and twenty-one. Walk between them and each throws your shadow a different way, one before you and one behind. Two shadows, one boy. He was a little disappointed and so was I.

Then he asked why the one in front had waved first, before he lifted his arm. I told him shadows on that bridge are known to be forward. I walked home across it with my hands in my pockets.

volumes.title: Lights Along the Marsh
volumes.text:
June, and hardly worth lighting lamps at all. I am the town lamplighter, and from number forty-one at the foot of Marsh Lane I can see clear across the marsh at dusk.

On warm evenings small lights come out among the reeds, low down, greenish, about the size of a thimble. I have seen marsh lights all my life. What I had not noticed before is that they travel in a line, evenly spaced, like a procession, and that the one in front goes slowest so the others can keep up.

Bryony Sedge, who cuts reeds out there, says it is the marsh counting its herons home. I asked how many herons. She said the same number as lights. I counted nineteen lights. I notice Bryony did not offer to count herons. Lamp forty-one was lit before I reached it. That is nine times now.

volumes.title: The Long Blue
volumes.text:
At midsummer in Emberwick the dusk does not fall so much as linger. The old people call it the Long Blue. I am Jory Flint, lamplighter, and on those evenings I sit on my ladder at lamp twelve with nothing to do until eleven.

It is said that during the Long Blue the Northern Fells walk down to drink at the river. They are simply nearer than they were.

I do not hold with it, but I am a careful man. From lamp twelve, at noon, the top of Cold Pike sits one hand’s breadth above the mill roof. I measured again at half past ten, in the blue. Two hands, and a thumb. I could make out single sheep. By morning it was back where it belonged. I have put both measurements in the book. A hill is entitled to a drink, the same as anyone.

volumes.title: The Owl on Lamp Seven
volumes.text:
A sighting of my own, and a nightly one. I am the lamplighter of Emberwick, and since the middle of July I have not been allowed to light lamp seven, by the corn exchange, without permission.

A white owl sits on the crossbar. She arrives at dusk as I do. If I set my ladder against the post she looks down at me, and does not shift, and I cannot reach the glass past her. I tried waiting. I tried coughing. On the fourth evening, feeling foolish, I took off my cap and said good evening. She stepped aside at once.

It has been so ever since. No greeting, no lamp. The corn merchants have started raising their hats to her as well. She does not move for them. She will be civil to the public, but she has business only with the man who brings the light.

volumes.title: A Door in the Hawthorn
volumes.text:
September. Three children of Tanner’s Row came in a body to me, Jory Flint, lamplighter, for my book of things seen at dusk. They had found a door in the hawthorn hedge behind the tannery. It is there only at sunset, they said, tall and golden, and gone by the time they fetch a grown-up.

I am a grown-up, so I went early and waited. They are right. At the back of the hedge is a gap where an old gatepost stood. For six minutes in the middle of September the setting sun comes straight through it and stands a door of light on the grass, threshold and all.

I timed it on three evenings. Then I told the children the hour at which their door opens. I did not tell them it was only the sun. I am not certain that it is only anything.

volumes.title: What the Fog Brought
volumes.text:
Reported to me, Jory Flint, lamplighter, at lamp thirty, by Sam Wherry the carrier, while I was up the ladder and the October fog was down to the rooftops.

He was driving in along the Grey Coast road at dusk. The sea is nine miles from Emberwick. All the same he heard a harbour bell, close by, slow, and then the creak of a rope. His horse stopped of its own accord. Above the hedge, he says, a ship’s lantern went by, swinging gently, as high as a mast would carry it, and passed inland over the turnips. A voice called out a depth. It sounded pleased with the answer.

I would doubt him, but I lit thirty-one and thirty-two in the same fog, and my coat was wet through afterwards. I licked my sleeve, which a lamplighter may do in private. Salt.

volumes.title: The Fourth Window
volumes.text:
November dusk comes at half past four, and I am out with my ladder before most of Emberwick has had its tea. I am Jory Flint, the lamplighter. This sighting is the miller’s boy’s and afterwards mine.

The old mill by the river has three windows on the side that faces the lane. Anyone can count them by day: three. The boy swears that at dusk, in winter, there are four, and that the fourth is lit, warm and yellow, with a geranium on the sill.

I have counted on eleven evenings. Nine times, three windows, dark. Twice, four. The fourth sits between the second and the third as if it had always been there, and somebody inside was laying a table. I did not go nearer. One does not stare in at windows, whichever sort they are. I raised my cap and got on with number thirty-five.

volumes.title: Going Round Backwards
volumes.text:
For most of a year, lamp forty-one at the foot of Marsh Lane has been lit before I, the town lamplighter, could reach it. I have counted sixty-three times. In January I decided to catch whoever, or whatever, does it.

I went my round backwards. I started at forty-one, in the last of the light, and it was dark and cold and ordinary. I lit it myself and worked my way up through the town to finish at number one, by the library gate. Number one was burning when I got there, the glass shut and the wick trimmed.

So it is not a matter of Marsh Lane. Whatever it is lights my last lamp, wherever my last lamp happens to be, so that I need not finish in the dark. I stood under it for some time. Then I said thank you, to the street in general.

volumes.title: The Apprentice’s Taper
volumes.text:
This is my last entry in the book of things seen at dusk. I am Jory Flint, lamplighter, and tonight I saw who lights my final lamp.

I hid behind the pump on Marsh Lane. At dusk a girl came down with a taper tied to a bean pole: Nettie Cooper, aged ten. She has watched my round from her window all winter, and my knee, and thought the last lamp was one too many for it. She wants to be a lamplighter. I have taken her on as apprentice, at sixpence and a ladder of her own.

Nettie began in October. The lamp was first lit ahead of me in March. I have written down both facts and do not intend to make them fight. The book is hers now. She saw a hare bow on the churchyard wall at dusk. I have told her to put it in.
